claim: Search statistics (depth, breadth, speed) do not separate masters from ordinary players; what separates them is memory for meaningful positions (about 93% vs 33% for novices).
agent_test: Qualified: flat search holds for easy positions; Campitelli and Gobet (2004) found nodes and depth rising with Elo on hard ones (N = 4). Do not cap search depth.

claim: Patterns on the board are tied to plausible moves and trigger the search; masters notice good moves quickly, then spend minutes verifying.
agent_test: Add a quick candidate-proposal pass before expansion; measure whether the verified move comes from the first-pass list.
audit_note: Simon & Chase text matches (patterns tied to plausible moves, masters notice at a glance then analyse minutes; 3-4 minutes per move; 50,000 chunks); Gobet & Simon say Kasparov's simultaneous play was 'often less than 100 points below' tournament level (worked example 2650 vs 2750), so 'about 100' is a mild rounding.

claim: Recall advantage is large for game positions and small for random ones (masters about 21% random vs about 92% game), so the expert edge is structured knowledge, not raw capacity.

claim: Concurrent visuospatial or executive load cuts chess recall (about 48-60% for strong players in Robbins 1996, over two thirds in the second-hand Bradley figure) and tactical move quality (about 37%); verbal suppression does nothing. claim: Pattern-match first answers block better solutions even in experts: a familiar solution cut candidate masters to the level of players about 3 SD (about 600 Elo) lower; 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose the familiar suboptimal move; the effect vanished when the familiar move was a blunder.
agent_test: Force one alternative-search step with a different cue after a plausible first answer; test on problems with a good but suboptimal obvious answer.
audit_note: Bilalic et al. (three SD, about 600 Elo, candidate masters performing like average players) and Sheridan & Reingold (8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose the Einstellung move; all experts avoided it when it was a blunder) both verified; the 3 SD figure is from a single pooled comparison in the 2008 series.

claim: Eye tracking shows the Einstellung effect is an attention bias: players hunting for a better solution kept fixating squares of the familiar one (no change across six time periods, F(5,20) = 0.6) while those without it shifted to the new squares (F(5,20) = 11.9).
agent_test: Check which features the second pass attends to; require a new cue, not a rewording of the first.
audit_note: F(5,20)=0.6 (ns) for the group with the familiar solution and F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001 for the group without verified in Bilalic et al.; Sheridan & Reingold replicate the gaze persistence; 'attention bias' is the authors' interpretation, from a small sample (about 5 players per group in the interaction test).

claim: In LLM reasoning, search beats best-of-N on harder items but not easier ones: on MATH, PRM-guided beam search was worse than best-of-N in the two easiest model-specific difficulty bins and better in bins 3-4, and choosing the method by estimated difficulty cut test-time compute by more than 4x; on Game of 24, Tree of Thoughts (b=5) reached 74% at about the completion tokens of 100 CoT samples, versus 49% for best-of-100 CoT (single-sample CoT: 4%).
agent_test: Gate search on estimated difficulty; skip it where the first pass is likely right.
audit_note: Snell et al. numbers are right (more than 4x compute saving; beam search over-optimizes on the easy bins 1-2 and helps on bins 3-4) but the bins are model-specific pass@1 quantiles, not MATH levels; Yao et al. Table 7 shows ToT's 74% costs about as many tokens as 100 CoT trials, whose best-of-100 reaches 49%, so setting 74% against single-sample CoT's 4% is not a matched-budget comparison.
claim_before_audit: In LLM reasoning, search beats a policy-only pass on hard items but not easy ones: beam search worse than best-of-N on MATH levels 1-2, better on 3-4; difficulty-chosen compute cuts cost about 4x; Tree of Thoughts 74% vs CoT 4% on Game of 24 at the tokens of about 100 samples.

claim: A gated fast-then-slow agent cut tokens per action to 757 vs 1,971 (ReAct) and 2,983 (Reflexion) while scoring higher on ScienceWorld; retrieved thought templates reached 82.4% on Game of 24 at about 12% of multi-query cost.
agent_test: Compare recognition-first with escalation against always-search at equal tokens on a single-answer reasoning set. Not yet measured in that form.

claim: Template retrieval with filled slots is measurable in LLMs (Buffer of Thoughts, held-out instances of the same families) but no study isolates slot-filling or tests transfer across task families.
agent_test: Build a slot-template store; test transfer to unseen families with and without slots.

claim: LLM chess at scale: deeper reasoning helps and wider sampling does not (up to +15% and +20% win rate from effort; 3x/5x mixture-of-agents flat); no LLM beat Maia-1100; o3 55.6% on puzzles vs under 15% for others; RL plateaus at 25-30% puzzle accuracy from missing chess knowledge. Studies do not use equal token budgets.
agent_test: Compare arms at equal tokens before using any of these as evidence for a design.
audit_note: All figures verified (LLM Chess +15%/+20% from reasoning effort, 3x MoA slightly above and 5x slightly below o4-mini medium on 30+ games; ChessArena no model beats Maia-1100, o3 55.6% and all others under 15% on puzzles; Hwang et al. 25-30% plateau with the authors attributing it to missing pretrained chess knowledge); caveat: the 'wider sampling does not help' point rests on one MoA setup with o4-mini.
